What held up:
- The facts in the three sources I opened are accurate. The Legit.ng loss, Zikoko's dead organiser and Wikipedia's no-legal-remedy point all check out.
- The cited stories span several countries and run from 2022 to 2026, so loss is not a few loud posts. I did not reopen the non-Nigerian ones.

What did not hold up:
1. Legit.ng: the post is from July 2026, but the loss was about three years earlier. It describes one daily collector who vanished. The article does not say it was a rotating group and does not mention records. "No written record is mentioned" is an argument from silence. A ledger would not have brought her back or recovered the money.
2. Zikoko: the summary I read says the article never mentions records, ledgers or receipts.
   - Only Dunni's case comes close to the claim, and that gap is about custody: nobody knew where the money was held.
   - Amaka's case is member default, Shubi's is an organiser diverting funds, Kingsley's is an online scam, and Daniel's cause is unclear.
   - In that summary, the organiser collecting first appears in only one account, so "often" looks overstated.
3. Wikipedia cuts against the framing. It says no records must be kept because no money stays inside the group. The candidate's entry shifts that reason to members seeing every transaction, then infers harm once visibility is gone. That inference is the candidate's, not the source's. In a pure rotating circle, the pot leaves each round, so a slot list covers most of what needs recording.
4. Four different things are merged into one problem: pure rotating circles, daily collectors, accumulating funds held by a treasurer, and Ponzi-style operators. Visibility complaints cluster in accumulating funds, such as the Kenyan welfare members demanding statements (snippet only) and the Tongan Christmas group (as summarised in the candidate's entry). Those are not ajo rotation. The headline figures, the $2 million and the 20 to 27 million pesos, are fraud cases, which the candidate admits a ledger cannot stop.
5. Research points to other causes. Search summaries of studies, not opened, attribute default to lump-sum consumption, multiple slots, dependants, income and the temptation to renege after payout. None of the results covered records. Prevalence is unknown: one Ogun State survey calls default high, while the candidate's Stokvel entry says defaults are rare.

What might rescue it: a narrower problem of honest treasurers of accumulating welfare or Christmas funds who want to prove they are clean. Treat that as a hypothesis until 2 or 3 real treasurers and members in a local group say so unprompted.

verdicts.reasoning:
Verdict: not refuted. Nothing blocks a one-day build, but the honest version is narrower than the pitch, and it does not stop most of the losses cited as evidence.

What passes:
- Data and APIs: no external API or data is needed. References are typed by hand, and AI is not needed, which also avoids the Gemini free-tier ban on personal data.
- Play policy: not relevant. It is a PWA with no sensitive permissions, and a WhatsApp link needs no install.
- Partners and approvals: none. The app holds no money, so the custody problem does not arise. I did not search for specific licensing rules on record-keeping tools, so that point is reasoned, not verified.
- Network effects: no marketplace. One treasurer brings one whole group, and one group is enough to be useful.
- Cost: Cloudflare Pages, a Worker and D1 fit the free tier.

Problems found, none blocking:

1. The ledger only shows what the treasurer typed. A member can catch their own missing payment early, which is real value. It cannot show that money exists. In the Mombasa case the treasurer gave members fake account details, and a typed ledger would have shown the same false picture.
The defensible scope is rotating circles only, where the pool empties each round and exposure is about one payout. Most headline evidence falls outside that scope:
- the N1,000 daily collector
- the Auckland $50,000 savings pot
- the Sh163,000 chama
- the Karachi and Nuevo Leon frauds
- funeral funds
The cost_of_problem figures therefore overstate what v1 prevents. The candidate admits part of this, but its evidence is still built on these cases.

2. Adoption sits with one person. Members who suffer cannot start it, and a dishonest treasurer never will. So v1 serves honest organisers who want to prove it. Search snippets of Pakistan HCI research also treated the organiser as the main adopter, but I could not read those papers. A scammer could also use the link as a badge of legitimacy, so the screen must say what it does not prove.

3. The described design has internal conflicts.
- Offline-first plus a read-only link needs a server, so the developer holds members' names and payment references.
- 'Locked at the start' blocks a build-day test, because a real group is usually mid-cycle. V1 must accept a mid-cycle start and agreed slot swaps.
- Members will not compare checksums by hand. The real protection is an append-only server log plus full plain-text summaries in WhatsApp, which every member holds.
- With no accounts, the treasurer needs a recovery code, or a lost phone ends edit access.
- Loans are in the problem statement but do not fit one day, so they must be dropped.

4. Data exposure grows with success. KPMG's summary of the NDPC guidance says processing more than 200 data subjects in six months makes an entity a controller of major importance, and the registration date has passed. That is about 14 groups of 15 (my arithmetic). This is not a day-one block, but a successful app would trigger it. A separate limb covers fiduciary holders of confidential information, and I could not tell whether this app fits it. Mitigations are nicknames, no phone numbers, and possibly storing only ciphertext with the key in the URL fragment. I did not verify that ciphertext storage changes legal status. Laws outside Nigeria were not checked.

5. Dependence on a solo developer. A record meant to outlive the organiser now depends on one developer keeping a free service alive. WhatsApp summaries and PDF export are the required fallback.

6. The build-day test depends on finding one real circle whose organiser agrees. That is likely if the author is in Nigeria, but it is not guaranteed.

Competition was not this lens, but it matters: AfroTools already has an ajo tracker with payout schedules, default rules and PDF export. Its page does not state price, storage or any member view, so the member-checkable view may still be the gap.

Research limits: 3 of 3 searches used. Four fetch calls were made and 2 pages were actually read. AfroTools failed once with a socket error and I retried it. The CHI PDF came back as unreadable binary and no PDF tool was available, so it is marked not opened.

Verdict: refuted as framed. Power cuts are a severe, recurring pain. The problem this app addresses, that nobody records what actually happened, has no complainant in the evidence, and its headline claim is contradicted by existing apps.

But this is a minister relaying small-business complaints on a TV show, with no dated incident in what I read and no named resident. 'Chanda' appears only in his remark, unidentified. The source is about 2.5 years old, and I did not check whether Zambia still has these cuts.
- Rawalpindi (devdiscourse, 27 Oct 2026): recent, with four named residents, and traders report losses and generator use. This is the strongest source, but it does not support the candidate's title because the article mentions no published schedule. The complaint is about unannounced cuts. The day's-notice demand came from one resident, Awais, not residents generally. The utility cites two hours of daily load management plus seasonal annual maintenance, so this may not be a steady state.
- GridWatch (CEGA): the 'nearly 100%' undercount and the 462 Accra sensors are confirmed, and smartphones are mentioned. The page names the Government of Ghana, MCC and the Berkeley researchers as the parties with an interest. It does not say households or businesses asked for outage records. It shows funders wanted measurement, not consumers.
- Citinewsroom and 3News were not opened because of the read budget, so those claims rest on the candidate's summaries. As summarised, the Ghana traders' union wanted a timetable to exist, which is the opposite of complaining that a timetable is wrong.

Why the pain does not transfer to this app:
1. A person in a blackout already knows the power is out. A log tells them, after the fact, what they just lived through.
2. Every demand in the evidence looks forward: advance notice, a timetable, or why the power is off and when it returns. Rawalpindi residents spent time contacting the utility to find out.
3. A single-phone history gives only a 'typical return time', and the evidence describes erratic timing, so that estimate would be weak (my inference).
4. Generator spending is a workaround for having no power, not for having no record. Under the brief's rule, money spent on generators does not count as evidence for a logger. I found no person, in any source, saying they want a record or keep one by hand.

'Nobody records' also fails on its face. Search summaries show Dumtraq (Ghana) tracks area outage history, Kanea (Ghana) tracks availability over time, and Power Failure & Outage Alarm (iOS) logs cuts and restores from a plugged-in phone, which is the same core method. NepaSituation and SOP Notify (Nigeria) and NERC's own reporting app also exist. I did not check any of these for usage or price. So the candidate's list of three schedule tools understates the field.

Best point in the candidate's favour: Nigeria, which is untested by the candidate's own evidence, may be a better fit. NERC ordered compensation for Feb to Mar 2026. Band A customers pay for a stated service level, so 'did I get my 20 hours' is a concrete job a log could answer. Even here, the compensation portal seen in summaries works from a list of feeders and a meter number, so a personal log does not appear to decide eligibility (my inference). No Band A customer in my results asked for a log.

Limits: all voices here come through news reports, so I have no first-person forum evidence. The Nigerian and app findings are search-level only.

What would change this verdict: five Band A customers in Lagos or Ibadan saying they would keep a log and use it to complain or claim. That is testable locally in a day, before any build.

verdicts.reasoning:
Not refuted, because nothing blocks a one-day build. It is still weak: build day delivers a record for one socket, not the planning help people complained about.

WHAT PASSES
- A single-phone logger needs no API, partner, licence, approval or two-sided market.
- It uses no SMS, notification or accessibility permission, so the Play Protect sideload block in the platform notes does not apply.
- Direct APK works during the challenge.
- Data stays on the phone, so legal exposure is small.
- PowerDetector on iOS suggests the charging-state method can ship as a product (listing snippet only).

WHAT BREAKS THE CANDIDATE AS WRITTEN
1. Background premise. GridWatch relied on charge events waking the app. Android's exception list contains neither power action, and a third-party GitHub issue says they cannot be declared in the manifest. Android's battery page still shows that manifest example with no Android 8 note on these actions, so the docs conflict. Plan on a foreground service holding a runtime receiver, with a permanent notification. That is fine on direct APK. On Play it becomes a declaration item, and specialUse needs a justification reviewers see, per the platform notes.
2. Local phones. A developer help page says Tecno's HiOS actively manages background activity. A 2019 forum report described a Tecno closing apps the user had whitelisted (search snippet only, my fetch failed). I found no current HiOS or XOS data. A killed service would read as no outages, which is the worst failure for a record app. This is the most likely point of failure, and only a soak test on a real device can settle it.
3. Coverage. The GridWatch paper says most phones are plugged in at night and calls daytime use a challenge. Trade losses happen in the daytime, so "leave a phone charging" really means a dedicated spare phone, and many users may not have one.
   My inference, not sourced:
   - An inverter-backed socket never shows the cut.
   - A generator-fed socket reads as power restored, and the evidence names generator users as the target group.
   - A phone that goes flat in a long cut loses the restore time.
4. Accuracy. An accelerometer-only filter gave no false positives, but the test was two phones for two weeks and three days, used routinely. The microphone hum classifier scored 87% in a limited sample, and the authors said phone detection alone is not enough for low error rates. The paper also says GridWatch had not been deployed at that point. A one-tap correction is therefore required, not optional. Cut the microphone filter on privacy and permission grounds.
5. Value timing. The complaints ask for notice and timetables, and a logger gives neither. "Typical return time" needs days or weeks of events. Forecasting from history also assumes a regularity the candidate says does not exist. A published schedule cannot be pulled automatically from any source found here, so planned versus actual needs manual entry.
6. Network effects. The neighbourhood page is empty with no users, and the paper flags that public data could reveal which homes lost power. Cut it from v1.
7. Safety, my inference, not sourced. Asking people to keep a device plugged in through restoration on an unstable grid may expose it to surges, and constant charging stresses old batteries. Say this in setup.

DAY 1 GATE
In the first two hours, run the unmodified logic on the cheapest Tecno or Infinix available. Leave the screen off, switch the socket off and on after a long idle period, and repeat overnight if possible. If events are missed, drop the idea rather than patching it live.

METHOD
3 searches and 3 successful page reads. One further read (Hovatek) failed and is reported as a snippet. The GridWatch PDF was read through text extraction of the saved file. Its page-level fetch summary failed, so passages were searched by keyword rather than read end to end.

verdicts.reasoning:
I tried to refute this and could not. The pain is real, recurring and recent, and the case for it is stronger than the candidate's own evidence suggests. Its sources are mostly from 2016-2017, and that was the obvious line of attack. It fails because of a source the candidate missed.

BEST EVIDENCE: RNID and SignHealth, 'Still Ignored' (2025). It surveyed 1,114 deaf people or people with hearing loss in England, with data collected 13 Nov to 26 Dec 2024.
- Being called from the waiting room was the most common barrier of all points in the patient journey, at 67%. Booking came next at 45%.
- By group it was 75% of sign language users, 80% of people needing a communication support professional, and 65% of people needing other adjustments. The table extraction was jumbled, but those three figures weighted by group size reproduce the 67% (my arithmetic).
- The report itself calls this a recurring experience. Its first-person accounts match the candidate's story closely: one woman missed her appointment, was told the next patient took her place, and did not rebook. Another met an irate doctor after telling reception she was deaf, and now dreads going back. A third, aged 75+, describes constantly watching for visual clues.
- The second, third and fourth quotes also show the same failed workaround: telling reception does not reliably work.

CITATION CHECK:
- Limping Chicken holds up. It says what the candidate claims, but it describes one anxious visit, and the author does not say she missed an appointment. A commenter does say they have.
- Healthwatch holds up, including the Dudley pagers, their use by people with other impairments, and the 10 Nov 2017 date. This is also spending evidence, because a real NHS trust adopted the pagers.
- I did not open deafinitelygirly, Southern Trust or Mayo, because the 3-read budget went elsewhere. Those claims, including the 2026 pilot, remain unconfirmed by me.

WHAT WEAKENS IT:
1. The 67% counts people who have ever hit this barrier, in a multi-select question. It measures prevalence, not how often it happens per visit. The candidate's 'every appointment' frequency is inferred, not measured.
2. The sample is self-selected, recruited through RNID and SignHealth channels and online.
3. The practical cost is less proven than the emotional cost. Missing an appointment was 21% of n=341, but that covers all unmet communication needs, not just waiting-room calls. A search summary gives 14% from a 2023 Healthwatch Buckinghamshire GP survey and 24% from an older RNID report, and I did not open either.
4. Per person this is occasional, a few healthcare visits a year, so it is painful but not daily.
5. Nearly all evidence is from England or the UK. I found no Nigerian or West African evidence, and my three searches did not target it, so local fit remains an assumption.
6. Nothing I read supports the pharmacy, passport office or barber extension. Treat that as untested.

MISMATCH BETWEEN PAIN AND APP (not fatal on this lens, but check it on the feasibility lens):
The app has the receptionist press the button, yet in the evidence the person calling is often the clinician. In the blog the GP called across the room, in the report a doctor came out to call, and other staff called from doorways. A receptionist may not know when the patient is being called. The evidence also shows staff failing or dismissing a simple request, so the app depends on the same cooperation that already breaks down. The solution must reach whoever actually calls the patient.

The 2025 report does not mention pagers or buzzers and has no specific waiting-room recommendation that I could find, so it confirms the problem but does not endorse this fix.

killed.title: Counter staff cannot tell a real mobile payment from a fake one

verdicts.reasoning:
Not refuted, but weaker than the candidate claims. Fake payment proof at the counter is real, recent and seen in several countries. The specific pain the app targets, staff who cannot see the account, is thinly evidenced.

What holds up:
- Three 2026 Nigerian police cases turned up independently of the candidate's sources: Ogun in May (N2,600 of food from a vendor), Edo in May (two bags of rice worth N150,000), and Jos in July (a provision shop). These come from search summaries; I did not open the pages.
- Police and guides in those results all tell sellers to check their own bank app before releasing goods.
- Nigerian developers are building fake-receipt detectors. That suggests the problem is widely noticed, but builders are not users.
- Rest of World (opened) confirms that unofficial apps generate receipts from a typed name and number, that merchants rely on screenshots because apps do not always notify them, and that a named Lima worker caught one by checking her own Yape account.

What does not hold up:
1. Overclaim on Business Today (opened). It never says writing down codes fails; it only describes the practice. It is a 2021 general trend report with no named victim, and its six-beers story is illustrative. Its stated remedy is giving staff real-time till data through the SIM or the M-PESA for Business app, which is an existing route.
2. Yape's "up to 30 a day" covers possible scams in general, not fake receipts specifically. The same article puts Yape at about 9 million users, so the figure does not show scale.
3. The Citi Newsroom source could not be verified. The fetch returned HTTP 500, and a targeted search did not find it. The candidate's own summary describes transactions not reaching accounts, which may be failed transfers rather than fake proof. The Accra trader who stopped taking MoMo should not count as evidence until someone re-reads it.
4. Frequency is not established. "Exposure on every sale" describes exposure, not incidence. No source says how often a given shop is hit, the cited losses are mostly small per event, and no overall loss figure exists.
5. The core mechanism looks misframed. The named victims appear to have had account access already: the Lima worker checked her own Yape, the Miraflores family checked their own app (per the candidate's summary), and the Edo trader was already asking about the delayed alert and accepted a network excuse. The documented failure is time and social pressure, not lack of access. Those people may not need a second phone to confirm; they needed to look before handing over the goods.
6. The absent-owner segment rests on one 2021 general article plus a line in Rest of World about showing fakes to employees. I found no staff member or owner in that segment describing it in their own words. Most victim accounts come through police or press, so the brief's own-words bar is barely met.

Net: the pain is real and locally testable, which is valuable for the series. Before building, confirm that shops with an off-site account holder exist in numbers and actually lose money this way. The app also adds a step to every sale to prevent an event of unknown frequency, and a phone call or WhatsApp to the owner already does the same job at almost no cost.

Limits: 3 searches used. 3 page fetches attempted, 2 succeeded, 1 returned HTTP 500. RPP, The Star, WithinNigeria and Desidime were not re-opened, so those claims are unverified here.
competitors: M-PESA for Business app gives staff till data if the owner sets it up (named in Business Today; cost not found)
A Nigerian fake transfer receipt detector built by a 16-year-old developer, seen on DEV Community (search result only; cost not found)
A phone call or WhatsApp message to the owner: near-zero cost, and the same confirmation step Counter Check formalises

verdicts.fatal_issue: The rewritten app reproduces a free WhatsApp or phone-call loop with the owner, keeps the same dependency on the owner answering in seconds, and offers no demonstrated capability gap. In Kenya, the cited worst case, operator and cashier logins let staff see payments directly and remove the owner from the loop.
verdicts.reasoning:
Refuted. The rewritten Counter Check is not competing with soundboxes any more. Its loop is: staff tell the owner the amount and name, the owner checks the real wallet, the owner replies. A WhatsApp message or phone call already does that for free on phones both people own, and "phoning the owner" is on the candidate's own workaround list.

What the app adds over WhatsApp is a tidier request, a full-screen green or red result, a spoken amount and a day log. That is convenience, not a new ability. It keeps the weakness that lets the scam work, because the sale still waits on an absent owner answering within seconds. None of the candidate's evidence, and nothing I found, shows anyone complaining that a WhatsApp or call loop fails in a way this app fixes.

The candidate's stated gap also cancels itself. It says staff access through a business app depends on the owner setting it up and on data. Counter Check depends on exactly the same two things, and needs data on two phones.

The worst case cited, a till SIM held by an absent owner in Kenya, has a first-party fix that is better because it removes the owner from the loop:
- Safaricom's M-PESA Business app lets a till add assistant operators, who get their own ID and PIN on their own number, with restricted functions. It shows collections and statements. This comes from search snippets only, because the Safaricom FAQ returned 403.
- Third-party pages disagree on whether operators can withdraw money, so the risk of giving staff access is unsettled.
- Kopokopo's Cashier role, which I read, lets staff request, claim and view payments without moving money. It adds attribution per cashier, which a shared owner-reply app does not.

Solo traders, who are the Accra and Nigerian POS cases, get nothing from Counter Check. The candidate admits this. Their free fix is checking their own app before releasing goods, which is the standard advice in the 2026 Nigerian guidance I read.

Fair points for the candidate:
- Two general searches found no dedicated staff-confirmation product. The Nigerian guidance names no tool, only the generic banking app.
- A real gap may exist for shops whose money lands in an owner's personal bank account with no staff login. Personal banking logins cannot safely be shared, so the owner must stay in the loop.
- Even there, the rival is WhatsApp, and the gap is unproven.

Limits of this check: I used 3 searches and 3 reads, and one read failed with 403. I did not separately query Google Play, Product Hunt or GitHub. Yape and Nequi business or employee features went unanswered because the search returned nothing on them. Whether Nigerian wallets such as Moniepoint or OPay offer staff logins or soundboxes was not established; absence from one search is weak evidence either way. Those unknowns could only add competitors in Peru, Colombia or Nigeria. They could not remove WhatsApp as the free substitute, so the verdict stands.
competitors: WhatsApp message or voice note to the owner: free apart from data (general knowledge, not sourced in this run). Same human loop as Counter Check, already installed on both phones.
Phone call to the owner: airtime only. Already on the candidate's own workaround list.
Owner or trader checking their own wallet or bank app: free. Standard advice in 2026 Nigerian merchant guidance, and sufficient for solo traders.

M-PESA Business app assistant operators (Safaricom, Kenya): staff get their own login and see collections and statements with restricted functions. Fee not confirmed; the FAQ returned 403, so this rests on search snippets.
Kopokopo Cashier role (Kenya): staff request, claim and view payments, and cannot move money. Pricing not listed on the page read.
Rented hardware soundbox (Paytm, India): Rs 29 rising to Rs 135 a month, from the candidate's cited merchant complaint. Disputed charges, but people pay for it.
Provider payment APIs such as M-PESA Daraja and MTN MoMo: named only in a search summary, not verified. Server-side confirmation suits developers, not ordinary shopkeepers.
Kolonell (Nairobi vendor): sells server-side payment verification per its own blog. Pricing not checked; a developer-side pitch, not a counter tool.

verdicts.fatal_issue: No free, legal, wallet-agnostic feed exists to show what actually arrived, so v1 makes the absent owner the data feed, answering by hand on every sale. That is the existing 'phone the owner' workaround with a better screen. It is weakest in the candidate's own worst case, where the owner is away and the shop is busy. Safaricom's M-PESA Jumbe now gives Kenyan staff direct alerts, which takes away the candidate's clearest case.
verdicts.reasoning:
The build itself is not the blocker. A PWA with a Worker, D1 and web push fits in a day. It needs no Play review, restricted permissions, partners or marketplace, because pairing happens inside one shop. It holds no money, so I see no licensing issue, though that is my reading and I did not check it with any regulator.

What blocks it is the data. The platform research rules out SMS, notification and Accessibility access. Provider webhooks would need merchant-level integration per provider, which breaks the 'any wallet' claim and does not fit one day. So the rewrite replaces the data feed with a person. The candidate itself lists phoning the owner as a current workaround. WhatsApp would do the same job with no install or cost, though that is my inference and not sourced. The green screen, spoken amount and day log are real but small additions.

It fails hardest where it matters most. The candidate's worst case is a till SIM with an absent owner. That owner must notice a push, open a wallet or bank app, find the credit and tap, within seconds, on every sale, including rush hour, when the candidate's Star source places some of these tricks. I found no evidence on how fast owners really answer. This is the deciding unknown and it remains untested.

Delivery has no timing guarantee either. web.dev describes Urgency only as a hint that lets the push service save battery, and it promises no real-time delivery. A Firebase snippet says Doze can delay delivery, but that covers Android FCM generally and I am inferring it applies to web push. I did not test this on low-end phones. Both phones also need data at the moment of sale.

Some of the listed scams pass through. A reversal after the goods leave gets a correct Received. A forwarded real confirmation, or a second sale at the same amount, can match an earlier genuine credit, because staff enter only amount and name, with no transaction ID. In the other direction, a pending genuine transfer would produce a full red, spoken screen in front of an honest customer. That safety risk is my inference.

The market has also moved. tech-ish (19 Oct 2026) describes M-PESA Jumbe: owners nominate up to 50 staff through *234#, and staff get amount, reference and time directly, on basic phones over SMS and USSD, with no owner tap. That is the Kenyan till-SIM case in the candidate's 2021 source. Caveats: the article gives no fee and no launch date, does not address fake-SMS fraud, and says Safaricom does not guarantee delivery times. It covers Kenya and Safaricom only, so Ghana, Nigeria and Peru stay open. For Nigeria, a search snippet from a soundbox vendor says its device listens to OPay, Moniepoint, MTN MoMo and Paystack webhooks. That is marketing, and I could not open the page.

What would overturn this: one real shop with staff, where the owner answers nearly all checks within about 30 seconds across a full busy shift, and still prefers this to WhatsApp afterwards. That threshold is my suggestion.

Budget: 3 searches used. 2 pages read. The Kolonell page timed out on two attempts and returned nothing, so 4 fetches were attempted in total.
competitors: M-PESA Jumbe (Safaricom, Kenya): staff alerts by SMS and USSD for up to 50 recipients on basic phones, with no owner tap needed. The article read states no fee.
Phoning the owner: cost of a call, same human step as this app, and listed by the candidate as a current workaround.
WhatsApp message to the owner: no added cost and already on the phone. My inference, not a sourced claim.
Checking the account in the bank or wallet app: free. Osun police advise it, but it needs the account holder or their login.
Paytm Soundbox (India): one merchant reports rent rising from Rs 29 to Rs 135 a month, per the candidate's source.
Kolonell soundbox (Lagos): vendor claims webhook-based announcements for OPay, Moniepoint, MTN MoMo and Paystack. Price unknown, because the page could not be opened.

killed.title: Prepaid users cannot independently check where their data went

verdicts.fatal_issue: The headline claim, that users have no independent way to see where their data went, is contradicted by the candidate's own Kenya source and by the free per-app view in Android settings. Dedicated monitors also exist, and complaints continue anyway. The pain that is real is distrust of operator deductions, which a device-side counter cannot settle, and no cited person asks for a receipt or an independent check. If the receipt works, it mostly confirms the operator's background-apps explanation.
verdicts.reasoning:
Verdict: the frustration is real, but the problem as stated does not hold, and that problem is the one this app is built on.

WHAT HOLDS UP
- The NCC numbers are accurate on the opened page: 23,396 data depletion complaints in H1 2026 (MTN 12,212, Airtel 9,806, Globacom 1,373, T2mobile 5).
- Formal filings count as people spending time on the problem, so this is more than a few loud posts.
- Recent search results point to a continuing dispute: MTN denials, daily usage reports, and reported legal complaints and protest campaigns. I saw those only as search results and did not open them.
- So 'my data vanishes and I distrust the operator' is real, recent and recurring.

WHAT THE CANDIDATE LEAVES OUT OR OVERSTATES
1. Scale. Depletion is about 5.66% of the 413,587 complaints (my arithmetic). The article never ranks it as a top category. Overall, 98.38% of complaints were resolved, with no depletion-specific rate given. Formal complaints undercount a problem like this, but the number is less striking in context.
2. People in their own words. The cited evidence contains exactly one named complainant, Willice Ochieng in Kenya. The Kenya Times article names no one else and gives no loss figure. The techeconomy calculators article names no subscribers and quantifies no harm. The rest is regulator counts and operator statements.
3. The audit is old. 'No major issues' rests on a statement by the NCC chief, with no figures or methodology. The article dates it inconsistently (finished Q3 2024, or announced December 2024), so it is about two years old. It is not current proof either way.

WHY THE STATED PROBLEM FAILS
- The title says users cannot independently check, and the problem text says their figures come from the party they are disputing. The candidate's own Kenya source contradicts this: it points users to per-app views in Android settings (Settings, then Data Usage), which are device-side.
- Search also surfaced dedicated monitors: GlassWire, My Data Manager, Data Usage Monitor, and DataMeter (Play listing updated October 2026). One 2026 guide says the built-in screen covers most users' visibility needs.
- That guide also still recommends Datally, which conflicts with the candidate's snippet that it was removed in 2019. I did not resolve this.
- If device-side per-app numbers have been available for years and complaints still continue, lack of visibility is probably not the cause.
- 'Nothing described lets a subscriber cross-check' is an argument from silence. The opened article simply does not address it.
- No source shows a subscriber asking for an independent check, a per-app receipt or a dispute card. Their complaint is that the data runs out.

WHY THE REAL PAIN IS NOT RELIEVED
- The real pain is doubt about what the operator deducted. Only network-side records can settle that, and a device counter cannot.
- My search for people comparing phone counters with bundle balances found no Nigerian or Kenyan threads. It found South African, UK, Canadian and US forums. These are mostly undated and I did not open them.
- Those threads suggest the two figures differ for mundane reasons such as cycle dates and reporting lag. They also suggest phone figures carry little weight in a dispute, and one anecdote claims gaps above 30%. Treat all of this as anecdotal.
- So the app's balance comparison would likely produce false alarms, and the dispute card has no shown value.
- Where the receipt does work, it will mostly name background apps, which is the operator's own explanation. That leaves the distrust unresolved.
- Expiry loss (South Africa) is a separate pricing and policy dispute. A countdown does not fix it.

LIMITS OF THIS CHECK
- Budget used: 3 searches and 3 page reads.
- The SABC page and the Datally snippet were not opened.
- X, Reddit and Nairaland were not targeted, and search is US-only, so finding no local threads is weak evidence. There may be more first-person complaints than I found, though that would strengthen the drain complaint, not the need for an independent check.

The score of 4 credits the real underlying frustration and marks down the unsupported gap, the single named voice, and the weak link between the pain and what this tool can do.
competitors: Android Settings per-app data usage: built in, no extra cost
Operator daily usage reports (MTN and others): provided by the operator, cost not stated in the opened article
GlassWire Data Usage Monitor: cost not verified
My Data Manager: cost not verified; current per-app features reported as unverified by one review
DataMeter - Network Monitor: Play listing updated October 2026, cost not verified
Data Usage Monitor: cost not verified

verdicts.fatal_issue: The core job, seeing which apps used your data without trusting the operator, is already free in Android Settings and in several free apps. The only unique promise, checking the operator's figures, cannot settle a dispute because device counts and billing counts differ by design. The per-SIM split may also be unavailable to third-party apps.
verdicts.reasoning:
Verdict: refuted on the problem as stated. A narrow gap may remain, but I could not prove it.

The claim that users "cannot independently check" is wrong as written. Android's own data screen gives a free, on-device, per-app breakdown with no operator involved, and the candidate itself concedes Android shows totals. Free or cheap third-party tools go further:
- GlassWire: per-app graphs and spike alerts.
- Data Monitor: daily tracking, per-app stats and alerts, using the same usage-stats permission the candidate plans to use.
- Internet Speed Meter Lite: per-app history.
- Data Saver: Usage & Blocker: per-app foreground and background split per billing cycle.
- My Data Manager: a search summary says setup offers recurring or pre-paid plan types.
So per-app usage, the foreground and background split, and alerts all have existing equivalents. Only the pricing and dispute layer does not.

Two findings weaken what is left of the pitch.
1. The independent check is weaker than pitched. The May 2026 review I read says tracker totals often differ from carrier totals because carriers count at the billing layer, and it calls carrier apps the authoritative billing source. A before-and-after balance comparison or dispute card will therefore show differences with innocent explanations and cannot show who is right. That is a limit of device data, not a gap competitors missed.
2. Per-SIM receipts may not be buildable. In November 2020 GlassWire staff said newer Android reports mobile data as a total across SIMs, and that they tested on a dual-SIM phone and found per-SIM counting not feasible. This is old and comes from one vendor, and I did not check it against current Android docs. Device Watch shows the active data SIM on dual-SIM phones, so logging the active SIM could be a partial workaround, but that is untested. The candidate promises per-SIM output, so this needs checking before any build.

The remaining gap: no source I read shows a tool that prices usage at what the user paid per GB, counts down bundle expiry, flags overnight idle use, or produces a shareable card. That is absence from secondary sources, not a demonstrated gap. The review simply does not cover those features, I read no Play listing, and My Data Manager's pre-paid mode may cover part of it. Even if the gap is real, it is a presentation layer over data that is already free. My inference, not evidence: complaints probably persist because people do not know these screens exist, and a new app from a developer with no audience does not fix that.

Soft spots in the incumbents, which do not overturn the verdict: the newest My Data Manager APK seen in search was June 2023, and a search summary mentions early-2026 GlassWire forum reports of crashes.

Evidence limits. I used 3 searches. Of 7 fetch attempts, 3 returned content, which is the 3-read budget. The My Data Manager Play listing, the F-Droid page and the GitHub repo all failed, as did one alternate URL for the review, so F-Droid, GitHub and DataMeter details come from search snippets only. I did not try to get around the f-droid.org block. The review has reliability problems: it lists Datally as a live free app, which conflicts with the candidate's snippet saying Google removed it in 2019, and its GlassWire Pro price of $4.99/yr conflicts with GlassWire's own forum saying all Android features are free. Treat its prices as unconfirmed.
competitors: Android built-in Data Usage: free. Per-app breakdown and per-line limits on the device, and it needs no install.

GlassWire for Android: free. GlassWire's forum says all Android features are free, but a May 2026 review lists Pro at $4.99/yr, so the price is in conflict. Per-app graphs and spike alerts. Staff said in 2020 that plans cannot be tied to a SIM.

My Data Manager (Mobidia): free with ads, Pro $4.99/yr per the review. Per-app tracker, alarms, and recurring or pre-paid plan types per a search summary. Current status unconfirmed; newest APK seen in search was June 2023.
Data Saver: Usage & Blocker: price not confirmed. Per-app foreground and background split per billing cycle, plus per-network blocking. Cannot run alongside a conventional VPN client.
Data Monitor (drnoob, F-Droid and GitHub): open-source project, cost not confirmed from a page I read. Daily tracking, per-app stats and usage alerts; requests PACKAGE_USAGE_STATS.
Device Watch (F-Droid): cost not confirmed. Counters per day or per billing cycle with a set start day; shows the active data-SIM carrier on dual-SIM phones.
DataMeter - Network Monitor (Play): price not confirmed. Per-app consumption, threshold alerts and daily target notifications.
Internet Speed Meter Lite: free with ads. Per-app usage history.
3G Watchdog Pro: free with ads, Pro $3 one-time. Per-day and per-month limits.
Operator tools (daily usage reports and calculators, per the candidate's own sources): free, but from the party being disputed.

verdicts.reasoning:
VERDICT: Not refuted, but the pitch does not survive as written. "Per SIM" must be cut, and the app cannot act as proof against an operator. A smaller app is buildable in a day, with build-day testing in Nigeria.

WHAT HOLDS
- Data source: the querySummary docs, current through the Android 37 reference (page updated 2026-10-28), say results are "Not aggregated over state, uid, default network, metered, or roaming". So per-app rows with a foreground and background split are available from one call, over any start and end time.
- No backend, AI bill, partner, operator approval or network effect is needed. Prices are typed by the user. One user's receipt is useful on its own.
- Regulatory exposure is low because nothing leaves the phone. The main legal risk is a shared card that implies an operator cheated. The brief's positioning handles that if the card states that device and operator counts can differ.
- Usage access: the search summary said PACKAGE_USAGE_STATS will not be granted to third-party apps, so no regular app can read other apps' stats. I reject that reading. It leaves out the user grant through Settings (my recollection of the docs, class page not readable), and shipped monitors such as Data Usage Monitor reportedly rely on Usage Access for per-app figures. Real apps prove the route works, more than the docs I could read do.

WHAT FAILS
- Per-SIM receipts. Since API 29 the subscriberId is guarded, and apps that do not meet the requirements pass null "to receive usage for all mobile networks". The app I read about does not get a per-SIM figure this way. I did not read the exact requirements in TelephonyManager; from memory they are privileged or carrier level, which a sideloaded app will not have.
- This matters beyond the feature list. Dual-SIM use is common in the target markets (my assumption, no source read). Anyone who ran data on two SIMs in a bundle's window gets a merged count, which distorts the price per GB and the balance comparison. The app must say so instead of hiding it.
- "Independent check" is partly oversold. The device count is independent of the operator, but it is not the operator's billing count. The opposite balance figure must be typed by hand, because SMS reading is ruled out by the brief's permission research. A gap between the two is a question to ask, not proof. No reconciliation tolerance is established, so the app should show the gap without judging it.
- "Idle overnight" needs a scope cut. True idle detection needs more work. A user-set sleep window is the honest day-one version.

UNVERIFIED RISKS
1. Sideload friction. The brief notes Android 13+ restricted settings can lock settings "such as accessibility". The candidate's line that usage access avoids the three blocked permissions does not cover this lock. I recall AOSP extending it to usage stats on Android 15+, but my fetch of that source failed, so this is unconfirmed. It would add a step, not a block, though it could lose non-technical users.
2. Low-end phones. I did not confirm that the usage access screen exists and works on Android Go or Tecno, Infinix and itel builds. These may be the most common test phones. If the screen is missing, those users get nothing.
3. History depth and time resolution. The page I read gives neither. If history is deep, a first run shows past days, which is a strong build-day demo. If buckets are coarse, the sleep window is approximate.
4. Play policy. Search found no current Play rule on PACKAGE_USAGE_STATS either way. Play production cannot happen in the 10 days anyway, so this does not block the challenge. Listed monitors suggest it is allowed.

WHY 6: the build itself is easy, but the headline feature fails, the comparison is weakest for dual-SIM users, and the install and grant path was not tested. For the competition lens: the built-in Android screen and several monitors already show per-app use. Only bundle pricing and the balance comparison are left as differentiators, and the candidate's claim that nothing fills this gap looks weak.

PROCESS: 3 searches. 4 fetch calls: two on the official class page returned only navigation, one on an AOSP URL I built myself returned 404 and no page, and one on the Microsoft mirror of the Android docs returned usable text. I did not count the 404 as a read. Official-page and policy facts here come from search summaries or the brief, not from my own reading.
competitors: Android built-in Data Usage screen: free, no install; a 2026 guide says it covers most users' visibility needs
GlassWire: free app described as a per-app data monitor; any paid tier not verified
My Data Manager: described as a simple tracker that aims to match carrier billing; cost and current controls not verified
Data Usage Monitor (Lufesu): per-app usage via Usage Access; cost not verified
DataMeter: per-app mobile and Wi-Fi tracking with custom alerts, per its Play listing snippet; cost not verified
Datally (Google): removed from Play in 2019 per the candidate's snippet, yet still recommended in a 2026 guide; status unresolved, cost not verified

killed.title: Snapchat's Memories export loses dates and locations and splits captions from photos

verdicts.reasoning:
Not refuted, but it survives only with a narrowed scope and one check before Day 1.

Research limits: two of my first WebSearch calls were cut off with no results and two retries returned results, so I stopped searching. The ToTheMax and Snatch READMEs were read after retrying. The GitHub topic page failed on both attempts, so its snippet stays unverified. No real export was inspected, so claims about export contents rest on one README summary.

Blockers I tried to find:
- Data and API: the input is the user's own export, so there is no key, fee or partner. Snatch says a Memories plus JSON export holds a json folder and a memories folder with photos, videos and overlay PNGs.
- Hard dependency risk: Snatch and ToTheMax still fetch through links in the JSON, and Snatch does this by POST to Snapchat's API. That leaves some doubt about whether every base file is really in the ZIP. If base media is link-only, a browser needs Snapchat to allow cross-origin calls, which I could not verify. A proxy is not a fix, because it would pass signed links to private media through the author's server, which kills the core promise and creates hosting liability. If a real export lacks base media and the links are blocked, this idea is dead as a local web tool.
- Legal: processing your own export locally with no login is low risk. No app name should use the Snapchat brand. Local-only also removes the liability of storing very private media, possibly including minors' images, which a server version would carry.
- Play policy: not relevant, because this is a web page. There is no AI, no marketplace and no network effect.

Real weaknesses, not blockers:
- Who can use it: the users are likely phone-heavy, and this is a multi-GB job. My assumption, unverified here, is that folder output needs desktop Chromium. Existing tools are also desktop, so buyers with a computer exist, but phone-only users stay unserved. That likely includes much of the West African audience, where multi-GB downloads also cost data.
- Build-day test: needs a real export, and the export wait is unknown. The cost of a missed test is high because the format has already broken one script. One sample captures only one format version.
- Partial solution: skipping video overlays leaves captions missing on videos, so the app solves the core job for photos and only the date for videos.
- Wrong export choice: a user without the JSON option selected must redo the export and wait, as ToTheMax's troubleshooting implies.
- Workload: ZIP reading, ID matching, EXIF writing, canvas merge, MP4 date patching, folder output and a report fit 8 to 12 hours, but tightly. Full test runs on large exports will take long, so test on subsets. Video GPS is cut because inserting metadata can shift file offsets (my assumption), and video burn-in is cut because the ffmpeg.wasm binary may exceed the 25 MiB Pages asset limit (size from memory, unverified).

Stale-format risk is ongoing maintenance, not a one-day block.
competitors: ExportSnaps: desktop for macOS and Windows, local processing, free up to 200 files, Pro listed at $9 or $14.99 one-time (sources disagree)
SnapEasy: Windows desktop app, $9.99, says it runs on the device (self-published claim)
SC Memories Importer: free iPhone and iPad app that imports the JSON and saves to Photos locally
Snatch: free command-line tool, composites overlays, needs FFmpeg for video
Snapchat-All-Memories-Downloader by ToTheMax: free, needs Python 3.10+, downloads with timestamp and location

killed.title: When the only carer is hurt, nobody else knows how to look after the person

verdicts.fatal_issue: The evidence shows carers lack a person to step in, not a way to record information. The app hands a manual to a stand-in that its own target users, by definition, often do not have. No first-person source I read reports a stand-in failing for lack of information or a carer struggling to write a plan.
verdicts.reasoning:
VERDICT: The fear is real and painful, but the candidate's stated problem (no handover information) is not what the evidence shows. The people quoted lack a person who can step in. Refuted on the specific problem.

WHAT HOLDS UP:
- The cited Alzheimer's Society thread is real, dated 24 Dec 2022, and matches the core claim. The poster went to hospital for a scan and had to bring a partner with FTD because nobody could sit with him.
- Ten distinct members replied, with first-hand patchwork arrangements, so this is not one loud post.
- A second, independent thread (28 Jun 2024) has a sole live-in carer asking the same thing.
- Search also surfaced similar titles on caregivers.com and Mayo Clinic Connect, so the worry recurs across forums. I did not read those threads or confirm their dates.

WHAT DOES NOT HOLD UP:
1. Wrong gap. The poster's words are about nobody being available. The 2024 poster asks who to call, whether social services step in, and whether care would be at home or in a care home. Neither asks how to record the person's routines. The one reply in 2024 describes social services arranging a nursing home the same day, which points to cover as the gap. That inference comes from one reply.
2. The target user defeats the product. The candidate targets carers with no family or neighbours nearby, then builds a manual for a stand-in. By its own definition, that stand-in often does not exist. A document helps once someone is there, such as a paid carer, an emergency scheme or social services. No source I read says a stand-in failed for lack of information.

verdicts.reasoning:
VERDICT: Survives, but only after a scope cut. The build is easy. What holds the score down is that the one-day version solves a narrower problem than the candidate claims, and removing custody also removes the anti-fraud layer.

BUDGET AND LIMITS: I used 3 searches and 3 fetch attempts. Only the Lagos law page opened, and it showed only section 1 plus the section headings. The PayIt2 and Minnesota AG fetches were blocked by a domain safety check, so those points rest on search snippets. No search result addressed Nigerian host liability for a page that never holds funds, so that question is still open.

CHECKS THAT PASS:
- Data and APIs: none needed. It is a small create/read/update web app with secret links. The researched Cloudflare free tier (Workers, D1, static pages) covers it at $0 plus an optional domain of about $12. No AI is involved, so the Gemini free-tier personal data trap does not apply.
- Play policy: not relevant, because it is a web link that needs no install or sensitive permissions.
- Partners and approvals: none, provided bank feeds and card payments stay out.
- Money regulation: no funds pass through the app, so a custody-based payment licence should not be triggered. This is my reasoning, not a legal opinion or a sourced finding.
- Network effects: none across collections. One organiser plus their own group is enough, so it works from the first user.

ATTEMPTS TO REFUTE, AND WHY EACH FALLS SHORT:
1. Lagos law. This is the most important new finding. The Public Collections (Regulation) Law makes an unregistered appeal for public collections unlawful, and section 1(3) puts the burden on the defendant to prove an appeal was not public. That matters because the author is probably in Nigeria and the candidate pitches medical and funeral fundraising. I could not read the exemptions (s.3), the definition of public (s.11) or the penalties (s.9), and I do not know whether a host is covered or how the law treats online appeals. Other Nigerian states were not checked. Singapore also regulates online benevolent appeals, including personal ones run through a crowdfunding platform, per a search snippet. A search snippet says the UK regulator does not cover personal-cause appeals. This does not block a private gift collection among people who know each other, but it does rule out presenting the app as an open public appeal tool until a lawyer has read the full text.
2. Fraud. Identity checks are the very step the candidate calls a structural failure, and they exist partly because of fraud. Search results show cloned GoFundMe pages and a Minnesota AG demand that GoFundMe remove imposter pages (snippet only). GoFundMe also advertises a donor guarantee. A free page with no login, no verification and free-text bank details is a ready-made scam tool on the developer's domain, and victims would have no recourse because nothing can be frozen. It does not fully refute the candidate, because a Google Form or a WhatsApp message with an account number can do the same harm, and one-day mitigations exist. A further risk, which is my inference: the researched plan puts all 10 apps on subdomains of one domain, so a fraud report against this app could hurt all of them. It should get its own domain or be easy to isolate.
3. Does it genuinely solve the problem? For small circles, yes. The Leetchi birthday case, the CollectionPot work and guest cases, and the fee complaints all disappear when the organiser is paid directly. It does not solve the GoFundMe-style cases if donors are strangers, who are unlikely to bank-transfer to an unknown person with no card payment or guarantee. So the medical and family-crisis half of the pitch only works inside a known circle. The self-reported ledger also proves nothing: received is whatever the organiser types, and real reconciliation needs bank APIs and partners. Trust therefore comes from the people knowing each other, not from the app. The bar is a WhatsApp list plus a banking app, and no evidence shows anyone asking for this tool.
4. Failure modes for the one-day build:
- Contributors leave to pay in their bank app and may never come back to tap, so the organiser adding payments by hand from bank alerts must be a first-class path.
- A leaked organiser link lets someone swap the bank details, so details need locking after the first pledge.
- Anyone with the link can post under a false name, so the organiser needs to remove entries.
- A lost secret link loses the ledger, since there are no accounts.
- Names, amounts and medical stories are personal data held by a solo developer, so a privacy page, a delete option and auto-expiry are needed.
All of these fit in a day.

BUILD-DAY TEST: Nothing depends on a country's payment rails, so it can be tested locally in Nigeria with any group. A real organiser must be lined up before the day. A real collection runs for days, so the episode can show the first confirmed payments, not a finished collection.

SOURCE CHECK

The OP calls it occasional but too frequent. No amounts are given. But this is one previously excellent client, the amount is not stated, and I could not confirm the candidate's 'paid on the day' detail. The most common advice was payment in advance. Nothing suggests either side was unclear about what was owed.
- Mumsnet 4483694 (Feb 2022): MISDESCRIBED. The OP is an adult pupil, not a parent, and is complaining as the client. The dispute is whether half a term's notice is fair after missing lessons with COVID and bronchitis. No written terms is confirmed. 'Nothing showing what was owed' is not supported: the amount was not the issue, the fairness of the charge was. I saw only part of this thread (19 posters out of 76 listed replies), so this applies to the visible portion.
- UK Business Forums: not opened. It appeared in my search results, but I never read it. The strongest claim in the candidate (chasing took more time than teaching) is therefore still snippet-only, and by the candidate's own summary that tutor already fixed it by taking payment at booking.
- Piano World thread: not opened and not re-found. By its title it concerns cancellations, not payment.

WHY IT FAILS
1. Cause: no opened source has a tutor or parent saying the balance could not be seen. Parents who owe generally know they owe. A private link showing the balance repeats what the cash book already did.
2. Severity: no opened source gives an amount. The opened complaints are about one client or occasional clients. Only one first-hand tutor quantifies impact even loosely, as regularly out of pocket.
3. Free fix: in the two payment threads, respondents repeatedly say to prepay, with one poster's rule being "No payment, no lesson". Search results for piano and music teaching show the same norm, including half-termly prepayment, late fees and pausing lessons. These policy examples are from search summaries, and I did not open them.
4. Breadth and recency: first-hand tutor voices across all opened sources number about 3 over 2020 to 2023. Most other posters are giving advice. The search aimed at 2025 and 2026 found few dated items. That is weak negative evidence, because I ran one such search, it did not target Reddit, and the search tool is US-only. It shows I found nothing recent, not that nothing exists.
5. Local test: Nigerian home-lesson tutors do exist per a Leadership report, seen only in a search summary. The arrears evidence I found is parents owing schools and governments owing teachers, not parents owing solo tutors. The West Africa claim is therefore unevidenced, though the test itself would be easy to run.

Paid products exist for this space. My Music Staff and TutorBird both offer a parent portal with an Account and Invoices view, and search results also mention automatic payment reminders, so some teachers do pay for parts of this. That supports a real general need. It also means the candidate's specific gap is already covered by existing products, contrary to its claimed narrower gap. A voice-teacher article on getting students to pay on time, also unopened, suggests the topic recurs. This keeps the score at 3 rather than 1.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE THIS
Recent first-hand posts from tutors who already prepay but still lose track of make-ups and block balances, or from markets where advance payment is socially hard to demand. That would be a different problem from the one claimed here.

3 WebSearch calls in standard mode. 6 fetch attempts: 3 returned content, 2 failed with connection errors and 1 returned 404. I counted only content-returning fetches as page reads, and the reads came through a summarising fetch tool rather than raw thread text.

2. Narrow. Function-level complaints I found total about four or five people: Geerling, toast0, possibly MrGilbert, a Slickdeals commenter and a homeownershub poster (the last two from search summaries only). At least three of these are Bosch. One incident on one product family is carrying the claim. The Consumer Rights Wiki entry appears to be about that same Bosch 500 issue, so it adds no independent victims.

4. Rare. A few purchases per decade per person, so nobody builds a habit or holds the pain for long. Reading the manual before buying is free, though imperfect, because the manual wording varies by model.

6. No local test. The candidate concedes no West Africa fit, so no real person can use it on build day.

Speed Queen purchases and the Dumb TV Index do show some money and time spent, but on avoiding smart machines generally, not on function-level lookup. Budget used: 3 searches, 3 page reads.
